synopsis: Generative models create realistic-looking images or sensor data; generated weather adds rain, fog, snow, dust or night to clear-weather recordings, potentially converting thousands of recorded hours into bad-weather data without waiting for winter [f12910, f12911]. Across chapters, the recommended role is training, failure discovery and wider test coverage—not stand-alone pass/fail evidence or a replacement for physically traceable sensor simulation [f93, f4871, f12922]. A 2026 on-road benchmark reported 94.8% realism acceptance for the best generative editor versus 26.3% for the best rule-based library, but this commercial, non-peer-reviewed preprint used a vision-language-model jury, and night-edit acceptance remained only 12.5–17.6% [f4447, f4878, f4894]. Visual plausibility does not establish sensor fidelity: generated images can violate radiance, geometry and cross-sensor consistency, while 2026 Waymo novel-view results of 13.19–20.82 dB PSNR were judged low fidelity for safety testing [f4904, f3758, f3822]. Experts disagree about generative world models as validation tools, quantitative off-road re-weathering validation was not found, and no standard or regulator treats generated weather as physically equivalent to real sensor measurements [f7442, f3825, f12919]. The recommended hybrid uses generation to propose tests while anchoring physics to models and measured weather-affected sensor behavior; labels such as “20 mm/h rain” or “50 m visibility” require calibration against real sensor data, otherwise their physical meaning remains unknown [f12923, f10888, f12921].
